brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: According to the Social Style model, what are the two axes used to classify buyer behavior?
choices: Introverted vs. Extroverted and Thinking vs. Feeling
Ask vs. Tell and Task vs. People
Aggressive vs. Passive and Emotional vs. Rational
Fast vs. Slow and Detail-oriented vs. Big-picture
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the X axis is Ask vs. Tell (how they get what they want) and the Y axis is Task vs. People (what drives their behavior).
questions.feedback_incorrect: The model uses two specific axes: Ask vs. Tell on the X axis and Task vs. People on the Y axis. These describe observable communication behavior, not personality labels.

questions.question: Which of the following is the signature question typically asked by a Driver?
choices: How does this work?
Why should I choose this solution?
What are the results?
Who else is using this?
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—Drivers ask "What?" because they are focused on results and outcomes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a signature question: Drivers ask "What?" (results), Analyticals ask "How?" (process), Amiables ask "Why?" (fit and relationships), and Expressives ask "Who?" (people and vision).

questions.question: What does an Analytical buyer's pressure behavior typically look like?
choices: They become argumentative and defensive
They take control of the meeting
They ask for more time and more data
They go quiet and withdraw
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—when Analyticals feel pushed, rushed, or uncertain, they pull back and request additional time and evidence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style shows a different pressure behavior when something breaks down in the conversation. Analyticals respond by asking for more time and data, while Drivers take control, Expressives become argumentative, and Amiables withdraw.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the primary foundation of the Social Style model?
choices: Psychological personality assessments and labels
Observed behavior rather than personality tests or psychology labels
Myers-Briggs type indicators and personality frameworks
Gut instinct and intuitive reading of people
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the model is built on observed behavior, which means you watch how someone communicates rather than relying on tests or assumptions.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Social Style model is deliberately built on observed behavior—what you can actually see and hear in how someone communicates. It is not based on personality tests, psychology labels, or gut instinct.

questions.question: Which selling tactic is most important when working with a Driver buyer?
choices: Spend significant time building rapport before discussing business
Present detailed data and logical evidence throughout the meeting
Respect their time by leading with conclusions and results
Focus on their vision and ambitions rather than specific outcomes
questions.feedback_correct: Yes—Drivers value time above all else, so you must lead with outcomes and end with clear next steps.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Drivers are task-focused and time-conscious. The approach that damages rapport with them is wasted time—unnecessary detail or small talk. Lead with results and clear options to keep their attention.

questions.question: What does it mean if a buyer shows both Amiable and Expressive characteristics?
choices: They are confused about their own communication style
They likely have an Amiable primary style with an Expressive adjacent style
They are not a real style and the model does not apply to them
The model predicts they will show unpredictable pressure behaviors
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—most people have a primary style and an adjacent style that softens or modifies how the primary style appears in real behavior.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Nobody is a pure style. Adjacent styles sit next to the primary style on the grid and modify how the primary style shows up. This explains mixed signals—if someone seems like almost but not quite one style, the adjacent style is likely the answer.

questions.question: What is the earliest warning sign that a style mismatch is occurring during a sales conversation?
choices: The buyer explicitly tells you their style preference
A pressure behavior or sudden drop in engagement appears
Your manager observes the call and provides feedback
The buyer requests a follow-up meeting instead of deciding today
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—catching these signals early lets you shift your approach before rapport is damaged, rather than rebuilding trust you didn't need to lose.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Early warning signs include a pressure behavior (taking control, asking for time, arguing, or withdrawing) or a sudden drop in engagement like shorter answers or less eye contact. Noticing these early is the key to recovering rapport.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the core difference between how you should sell to an Amiable versus an Analytical buyer?
choices: Amiables need data; Analyticals need relationship building
Analyticals need detailed evidence and time to evaluate; Amiables need rapport first and collaboration throughout
Amiables are task-focused; Analyticals are people-focused
Both need the same approach, just delivered at different speeds
questions.feedback_correct: Well done—Analyticals require rigorous process and evidence to feel confident, while Amiables need safety through relationship and "we" language before engaging in business.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Although both are lower on visible emotion, Amiables and Analyticals have completely different primary needs. Amiables need rapport and collaboration; Analyticals need logical rigor, evidence, and time. The selling tactic must match each buyer's core driver.

questions.question: What does versatility mean in the context of Social Style Selling?
choices: Having a different personality for each of the four buyer types
Being flexible enough to agree with any buyer's perspective
Deliberately adjusting your communication approach to reduce friction and connect more effectively
Treating every buyer the same regardless of their style
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—versatility is a disciplined, conscious adjustment that helps the buyer understand you, not a change in who you are.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility is not about pretending to be someone you are not. It is the deliberate act of adjusting how you communicate so the buyer does not have to work as hard to connect with you, making them feel understood and earning trusted advisor status.

questions.question: Based on the framework, what should you do first in a real sales conversation to apply Social Style Selling effectively?
choices: Launch into your pitch using your natural selling style
Ask the buyer to identify their own style preference
Read the observable cues, identify the style, and adjust your approach before pitching
Wait for the buyer to show pressure behavior so you know if you are on track
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—read the cues (especially the signature question and emotional level), name the style, and then adjust your approach. That disciplined habit is how versatility works in practice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The core habit is: read the observable cues, name the style (even just to yourself), and adjust your approach accordingly. This happens before you pitch, not after. Waiting for pressure behavior means you are already behind.
